title: Shiva cannot stir
hookLine: a long hymn to the goddess opens with a sentence about a god who cannot even stir

cards: A long Sanskrit hymn to the goddess, the Saundarya Lahari, the wave of beauty, opens in a strange place. Not with her face, her weapons or her lion.
It begins with Shiva, the great god of the mountain, the destroyer, the lord of yogis. And what stands out in that first verse is what he can't do. Without her, the verse says, he can't create.
He can't even stir. Tradition says the hymn comes from Shankara, the teacher of non-duality. Whoever wrote it chose to open a praise of the goddess with God standing perfectly still.

teach.h: JOINED WITH SHAKTI, SHIVA IS ABLE.
teach.b: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. Shiva, joined with Shakti, is able to create. If not, this god is not even able to move.
So how could anyone without merit bow to you, or praise you, you who are worshipped by Vishnu, by Shiva, by Brahma? First, the play on words in the Sanskrit.

teach.h: SHAKTI AND SHAKTA: POWER AND ABLE.
teach.b: Joined with shakti, power, the word this path first met in Durga's story, Shiva becomes shakta, able. The verse sets the two sounds side by side, and the second time the sound means capable. Second, the couple.
In the Puranas, Shiva and Parvati are married, with children.

teach.h: THE GODS THEMSELVES BOW TO HER.
teach.b: The verse doesn't deny that. But it says something sharper. She isn't only his wife.
She is the reason anything he does gets done. Stillness on one side, movement on the other, and nothing happens until the two are together. Third, the ending.

Vishnu who protects, Brahma who creates, Shiva who dissolves: in this hymn, all of them stand before her. Some who worship the goddess hear that line as the whole point. In their reading, power isn't a tool God picks up.
It's the face of God that acts. And a fourth, closer to home.
You can hear this teaching in how Hindus name the divine couples: Sita-Ram, Radhe-Shyam, Gauri-Shankar, the goddess first.

teach.h: WITHOUT HER, HE CANNOT EVEN STIR.
teach.b: Many teachers explain it this way: you come to God through his Shakti. And in a Shiva temple, the linga rises from a base many read as Shakti, the two worshipped together.

how: The Saundarya Lahari is chanted and studied by worshippers of the goddess, including in the Shri Vidya tradition, and a reading of it begins with this verse.

games.why: the wave of beauty starts with God standing still: joined with Shakti, Shiva is able to create; without her, he cannot even move.

practice: If there's a picture of Shiva and Parvati near you, or of any divine couple, look at it a while: the still one and the one who moves.
Then say a pair's name slowly, the goddess first, the way Hindu families do: Gauri-Shankar, Sita-Ram, Radhe-Shyam. If you pray, let the names be your prayer, one with each breath out.
If you don't, notice the stillness in you, and the breath that moves it.
